title: The Ponziani
description: This is the "Best Beginner Chess Opening" and for good reason. The plans are easy to learn and there are so many traps for Black to lose in 10 moves.

r1b1k2r/ppp1bppp/1n1q4/8/3n4/1BP5/PP3PPP.text:
Material is equal in this line.

But we will have an isolated queen's pawn.

r1b1k2r/ppp1bppp/1nnq4/8/3p4/1BP2N2/PP3P.text:
The queen recaptures so the bishop doesn't move again.

And we take on d4 with the knight.

We wanted to avoid Bg4.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qppp/2n2n2/1B2p3/3P4/5N2/PP.text:
They can still capture once, however.

We'll take back...

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qppp/2np1n2/4P3/3P4/5N2/PP3.text:
Black can open up the light-squared bishop and put pressure on e5.

It's impractical to defend the pawn with Bf4 now, so I suggest something else.

Bb5 essentially serves the same purpose as protecting the pawn on e5, as Black has one less attacker on it now.

r1b1kb1r/ppppqppp/2n2n2/4P3/3p4/2P2N2/PP.text:
Placing the queen on e7 early, in front of the bishop, seems illogical, but it is the third most popular move here, played 16% of the time.

Black pins our pawn on e5 to the king.

Capturing in the center is simple and natural. We take our pawn back and protect the center.

r1b1qrk1/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P1B1/8/1BP2N2/P4.text: The queen's only available square is e8.

After which we can play Re1.

We've got a big lead in activity and development and a winning advantage.

This initiative could transform into either an attack on the king, or a slow positional build up until we squeeze Black.

r1b2rk1/ppp1bppp/1n1q4/8/3P4/1BN5/PP3PPP.text:
We will try to limit trading pieces and use our pieces to move around the IQP. 

With the knight on c3 and bishop on b3, we can even consider pushing d5 safely.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/1nnp4/4P3/1b6/1BNQ1N2/P.text:
Expect Black to move the d-pawn at some point and challenge your e5-pawn.

However, ...d6 in this case is a mistake!

Remember that you can push the pawn to e6 in this position.

Why is this possible?

r1bq1rk1/pppp1p1p/1nn3p1/4P1N1/8/1BbQ4/P.text:
Black can defend against it, but the point of this line is to weaken Black's pawn structure.

We can additionally do that here with Qh3.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1p2/1nn3p1/4P1Np/8/1BQ5/PP3.text:
And only now can we capture on c3.

After this combination, Black's kingside structure is extremely weak and the g6-pawn isn't even defended by the f7-pawn, as it's pinned.

We'll look to activate the rest of the pieces and target those weak spots.

White's got a big advantage here.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1p2/1nn3p1/4P1Np/8/1Bb4Q/PP.text: Black is forced to play ...h5 if they don't want to give up the queen.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/1b6/1BN2N2/PP.text:
Black chooses to do the same.

Since they haven't captured the c3-knight now...

We can choose to protect it with the queen and potentially avoid our pawns splitting.

However, there is an additional point behind this move...

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/8/1BP2N2/P4PP.text:
If they try to play logically and castle, thinking they have no worries...

Suddenly Bg5 arrives!

This is why it's important for Black to move the d-pawn before this.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/8/1BbQ1N2/PP3.text:
If Black captures on c3, we won't recapture with the queen immediately.

We'll play Ng5 first and threaten checkmate!

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/4P3/3p4/1BP2N2/PP.text:
8...Be7 is the solid way of developing.

We will simply take on d6.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/1b6/1BN2N2/PP3.text:
One of the logical moves for Black is to pin our knight on c3.

Let's just bring the king to safety.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/8/1Bb2N2/PP3PP.text:
Black capturing on c3 can actually lead them into trouble.

We'll take back first.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn5/3pP3/3p4/1BP2N2/PP.text:
With this move there are nearly 3,000 games. 

Black wants central space.

We will take on d4 and get a big center.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn5/4p3/3p4/1BP2N2/PP3.text:
If the pawn takes on e5, we don't mind. 

Our goal is to open up lines and attack f7 and potentially the e-file.

We can begin to attack f7.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nnp4/4P3/3p4/1BP2N2/PP.text:
There are more than 2,000 games with 7...d6. 

Black wants to undermine e5.

We will simply castle and let them take on e5 if they want. We have e-file counterplay. 

If 8...Nxe5, we want to play 9.Nxe5 and then cxd4. We want to open up lines towards the king in the center.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B1pP3/4n3/2p2N2/PP.text:
That's why Black removes our pawn on c3.

We'll recapture with the knight in order to activate another piece.

Now Black's knight on e4 is under additional pressure.

Once again, if Black tries ...Bf5, Nd4 is strong.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B1pP3/8/2n2N2/PPQ2.text:
You will see a trade on c3 here most likely.

We'll take back with the queen to keep the pawns together and attack the knight on c6.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3n2N1/3p4/1B6/PP3PP.text: If the pawn recaptures, we've got a nice double attack.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3np1N1/3p4/1BP5/PP3.text:
Black can block the attack on f7 with their knight.

However, we will simply open up lines towards their king.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pP3/3pn3/2P2N2/PPQ.text:
Black goes ahead with their plan and protects the knight with ...d5.

Here, Black would like to play ...Bf5, which is why I don't recommend cxd4.

Let's instead develop the bishop and pin Black's knight on c6.

This way we threaten to capture on d4 with the knight in case Black plays ...Bf5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3np1N1/3n4/1B6/PP3PPP.text:
10...Nxd4 is a solid approach.

The centralized knight keeps the e-file closed for the time being, and it prevents our Qf3 move.

We will make use of the e-file to counterattack and claim some compensation.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3np1N1/8/1n6/PP3PPP/R.text:
This trade gives up a pawn. 

However, Black's point is that they're getting rid of our powerful bishop.

We take the pawn with check.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/2Bp4/2P2N2/PP.text:
It can rotate to the queenside and hit our bishop.

The b3-square is where we want to retreat to most of the time.

We did give Black a tempo in this small skirmish, through our bishop retreat.

7...Be7 allows us the calm 8.O-O, and we have ideas of playing 9.cxd4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/8/1Bp2N2/PP3P.text:
Our retreat allows them to capture our pawn on c3.

That's fine.

We'll recapture with the knight.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PP.text:
Black plays a rather natural move, attacking the center, which takes advantage of the fact that we can't defend the e4-pawn with our knight.

The Jaenisch Counterattack is played 45% of the time, in almost 8 million games.

We'll gambit a pawn on e4, but we obtain a strong center and put pressure on Black's e5-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/3pP3/2P2N2/PP3.text:
This study will deal with the most popular response for Black in this position, which is capturing on d4, played 66% of the time.

We'll unleash an intermezzo and push in the center with tempo!

This move takes advantage of the extra space immediately, prevents Black from capturing on c3 or on e4, and forces Black's knight to move!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/3nP3/3p4/2P2N2/PP3.text:
Played 32% of the time and in almost 600,000 games, 5...Nd5 is the most popular response for Black.

This move is played with a concrete goal of keeping the knight safe but active.

Capturing on d4 now could be played, but we give Black some chances after ...Bb4+. Instead, we attack the knight with Bc4...

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/3P2n1/5N2/PP3P.text:
We'll simply capture on d4, protect the pawn and maintain a massive center.

We'll play h3 next to kick the g4-knight away and already achieve a substantial advantage.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/3p2n1/2P2N2/PP.text:
5...Ng4 looks aggressive and is the second most popular move played 22% of the time.

It seems like Black is targeting the e5-pawn, but this gives us the freedom we strive for in the Ponziani.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/3pn3/2P2N2/PP3.text:
...Ne4 is played 14% of the time on move 5.

Black wants an active knight in the center and wants to play ...d5 to support it.

Of course, we can easily attack that knight while developing a piece, which is more often than not a good choice in the opening.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops and defends e5.

We play c3, the Ponziani, with the idea of playing d4 next.

This in turn can offer open lines and extremely active piece play down the line.

A downside could be that the c3-square is now occupied and we can't place a knight there...

r2q1rk1/ppp2p1p/1nnpb1p1/6N1/1b6/1BNQ4/P.text:
Black has to defend against checkmate, of course.

Now we'll cash in on the e6-square.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1nn5/3pP2b/1b1P4/1BN1BN1.text:
And now we castle: we will go g4 and Qe2 to connect our rooks. 

We should be happy with our strong central pawns.
But Black will usually go backwards to h5 and maintain the pin.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1nn5/3pP3/1b1P2b1/1BN1BN.text:
Black castles.

We would love to get that bishop pair.

r2q1rk1/ppp2ppp/1nnpb3/8/1b6/1BNQ1N2/PP3.text:
Once Black captures on e6...

There's the extremely strong Ng5.

Not only do we attack the bishop twice, but we also threaten checkmate on h7!

r2q1rk1/ppp4p/1nnpp1p1/6N1/1b6/2NQ4/PP3P.text:
Black recaptures.

And we'll take with the knight and a fork!

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/1nn5/3pP3/1b1P2b1/1B2BN2/.text:
Black speeds up development with this check.

But we can develop and block.

r2qk2r/pppb2Qp/2n1pb2/1B1p4/8/5N2/PP3PPP.text: There's an active defense for Black in the form of ...Bf6.

r2qk2r/pppb3p/2n1pb2/1B1p4/8/5NQ1/PP3PPP.text:
However, placing the queen on g3 is convenient for us, as it's safe there. Black most likely won't be castling kingside.

For the middlegame, active and natural moves are Bf4 to line up with the queen on g3 and hit the c7-pawn, and bringing the rooks to the center.

All in all, an interesting but equal position.

r2qk2r/pppbb1pp/2n1p3/1B1p4/8/2Q2N2/PP3P.text:
Black has no choice but to capture on e6 as the bishop was under attack as well.

And now we'll take on g7 and hit the rook in the corner.

r2qk2r/pppbbppp/2n5/1B1pP3/8/2Q2N2/PP3PP.text:
Black continues developing naturally, preparing to castle themselves. 

However, this bishop left its post on f8 and isn't guarding the g7-pawn anymore...

Which means that we can push e6!

Keep this trick in mind when there's a queen on c3. We give up the e-pawn in exchange for the g7-pawn.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn1b3/4p1N1/3p4/1BP5/PP.text:
The bishop can block.

We will take the bishop and get a pawn back.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/1nn5/3pP3/3P2b1/1B3N2/PP.text:
8...Bg4 pins our knight. 

And tries to undermine our defense of d4.

We will support d4 further.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4b3/3nR1N1/8/1Q6/PP3PPP/.text:
The engine suggest we give a check on b5 if we can before taking on b7. 

That's because we want to provoke Qd7 so that Qxb7 comes with a tempo. 

We have good open lines and we will also trade our knight for that bishop which is currently holding everything together.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4b3/3nR1N1/8/1n6/PP3PPP/.text: The bishop blocks, lending extra defense to the knight on d5 in the process.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/1nn1B3/4p3/6Q1/8/PB3PPP/R.text:
We recapture with the bishop. 

We will play Nc3 and Rad1 and Rfe1. 

Ne4 could also be a great follow-up to Nc3.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/1nn1B3/4p3/6Q1/8/Pp3PPP/R.text: If Black continues taking pawns, we have so much activity that the engine says we're equal.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/1nn1B3/4p3/8/2p5/PP3PPP/R.text:
Black can get greedy. 

But open lines are what we want.

Pawns aren't important in this variation: rather, getting our pieces active is what we must do.

r2qkb1r/ppp3pp/1nn1p3/4p3/3p4/1BP5/PP3PP.text:
Black recaptures.

We take on e6.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2n5/1B1pP3/8/2Q2N2/PP3P.text:
The most natural defense is with the bishop on d7.

This gives us the freedom to castle.

r3kb1r/pppbqppp/2n2n2/1B2P3/8/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
And now Black unpins the knight on c6.

It seems like our only options to save the pawn are to play Bf4, which is rather passive, or to capture the knight on c6.

However, we can castle our king!

The point is that Black can't afford to capture the pawn now because of Re1 problems, and now the threat of capturing on f6 is reintroduced.

r3kb1r/pppbqppp/2n5/1B2P1B1/6n1/5N2/PP3P.text:
We can simply develop our dark-squared bishop with tempo on the queen, and Black is in trouble.

Blocking with ...f6 leads to a disaster on the e-file after we capture, so Black has to play something like ...Qc5.

After that, we'll simply play Nc3 and enjoy an easy position and a winning advantage.

r3kb1r/pppbqppp/2n5/1B2P3/6n1/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
That's why jumping to g4 is the most logical for Black.

We don't have to worry about the e5-pawn for now, though.

r4Nk1/ppp4p/1nnp2p1/8/1b5q/2NQ4/PP3PPP/R.text:
But we've just won an exchange and have a huge advantage.

Try to remember this e6 trick when you've got the pieces set up in the right way.

r4rk1/ppp4p/1nnpN1p1/8/1b5q/2NQ4/PP3PPP/.text: Black tries to play actively with ...Qh4.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black responds with ...e5, the most popular first move for Black!

The knight comes out to its natural f3-square and attacks the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the first study of our Ponziani course.

In Chapter 1, we'll examine the Jaenisch counterattack, which is the most popular response for Black after 3.c3.

The idea is that Black plays 3...Nf6 to attack e4. 

Study 1 will deal with Black capturing our pawn on d4 after we advance in the center.

4rrk1/p1pp1ppp/1b3q2/8/2N5/2P1BQ2/PP2KnP.text:
We are just in time to cover the king up with our bishop.

At the end of this forced mess, the engine gives total equality, but it's Black who needs to play accurately in order to prove that this really is equal.

It's easy for Black to go wrong and White has great practical chances.

After all, we are up a whole piece!

4rrk1/p1pp1ppp/1b3q2/8/2N5/2P2Q2/PP2KnPP.text: And when Black gives a check...

N1b2b1r/p1k1nNpp/1q1p4/1B6/4n3/2P5/PP3PP.text:
And we finally capture the rook on a8, underpromoting our pawn to a knight and forking Black's king and queen!

Black should resign here.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2P5/2bQp3/8/2P2N2/PP3nP.text:
Black can also defend the bishop.

Against this, it's best to capture the b7-pawn and fork Black's pieces!

r1b1kb1r/p3nppp/1q1p4/1B6/3Nn3/2P5/PP3PP.text:
We can simply bring our knight back to d4, defending the bishop and opening up a discovered check.

A completely winning position. We are up a pawn and ready to castle. 

Whatever Black does, they'll be left with a weak king in the center of the board that's subject to attacks.

r1b1kb1r/p3nppp/1qNp4/1B6/4n3/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
Black's best try is to go for ...Qb6.

This attacks the b5-bishop and threatens checkmate in one.

Looks scary, but we have a move to deal with both of these threats.

r1b1kb1r/pp2nppp/1qPp4/1B2N3/4n3/2P5/PP3.text:
A tricky attempt is ...Qb6, attacking the b5-bishop and threatening mate.

This move, however, fails miserably and for quite a beautiful reason.

We can capture the b7-pawn and uncover a check from our bishop.

If Black now takes the bishop we can simply take on a8 and make a queen.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qpp1/3p2p1/3P4/4n3/2P1B3/PP.text: Black's most logical way to continue is ...d6, opening up the c8-bishop.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qpp1/3p2p1/3P4/4n3/N1P1B3/P.text:
And we'll prepare queenside castling with Na3. The knight can jump into c4 or b5 at some point in the future.

White is slightly better. We have more space and a lead in development.

r1b1kb1r/ppp1qppp/3p4/3Pn3/4Q3/2P5/PP2BP.text: Black's most logical way to continue is ...d6, supporting the knight and opening up the light-squared bishop.

And we can castle our king.

White is slightly better here. We have more space and superior development.

We can look to proceed with moves like Na3 and Re1, and should avoid any queen trades if possible.

r1b1kb1r/ppppqpp1/6p1/3P4/4n3/2P5/PP2QPP.text:
Black recaptures with the h-pawn.

We should then continue by developing our bishop to e3.

r1b1kb1r/ppppqppp/6n1/3PN3/4n3/2P5/PP2QP.text:
The other option is ...Qe7. 

This is slightly less popular, but still played roughly 33% of the time.

We'll proceed by taking the g6-knight.

r1b1kb1r/ppppqppp/8/3Pn3/4Q3/2P5/PP3PPP/.text:
Black now has to proceed with ...Qe7, defending and unpinning the knight.

We can continue naturally developing with Be2, preparing kingside castling.

r1bk1b1r/pP2nppp/1q1p4/1B2N3/4n3/2P5/PP3.text:
Black can attempt one final trick with ...Kd8. Make sure not to prematurely capture the rook and blunder mate!

There are many ways to win here, but one is more beautiful than the others.

We capture on f7 with our knight.

r1bq1k1r/p1pp1ppp/1bp5/4Q3/3N4/2P5/PP3nP.text:
And we can jump our knight into d4.

We're up a piece for two pawns and Black doesn't have a clear attack or way to regain the material.

r1bq1k1r/p1pp1ppp/1bp5/4Q3/8/2P2N2/PP3nP.text: Black really shouldn't trade queens, so the best course of action is ...Kf8.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/1bP5/3Qp3/8/2P2N2/PP2K.text:
Black's best is to castle kingside.

This is another piece sacrifice...

We can capture the b7-pawn and fork!

r1bqk2r/p1pp1ppp/1bp5/3Qp3/8/2P2N2/PP3nP.text:
Black's best is to capture the c6-pawn, preventing any cxb7 ideas.

We'll respond by taking the e5-pawn.

r1bqk2r/p1pp1ppp/2p5/4p3/4n3/2P2N2/PP2Kb.text:
Black can also capture the c6-pawn.

This is played roughly 28% of the time and isn't all that great for Black.

We'll proceed with Qa4, activating our queen and attacking the e4-knight, also stopping ...Ba6+.

r1bqk2r/p1pp2pp/2p5/4pp2/Q3n3/2P2N2/PP2K.text:
The knight can't move because it's defending the f2-bishop, so Black must defend it by advancing ...f5.

We can now go Nbd2, simply looking to trade off Black's key knight on e4.

r1bqk2r/p1pp2pp/2p5/4pp2/Q7/2P2N2/PP1BKb.text:
And we'll recapture with our bishop. 

White is crushing here. The bishop and the e5-pawn are hanging, and Bg5 is a serious threat to win Black's queen.

r1bqk2r/p1pp2pp/2p5/4pp2/Q7/2P2N2/PP1nKb.text: It is logical for Black to trade knights.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bP5/3Qp3/8/2P2N2/PP2Kn.text:
Black proceeds with ...Nf2, saving their knight and attacking our rook.

We'll go Rg1, saving the rook.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bP5/3Qp3/8/2P2N2/PP3nP.text:
Black can retreat the bishop to safety.

We'll respond by saving our rook.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bP5/4p3/4n3/2P2N2/PP2K.text:
Usually, Black retreats the bishop.

We'll move our queen to d5.

This move attacks Black's knight, but also potentially enables us to capture the b7-pawn at the right moment.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2P5/2b1p3/8/2P2N2/PP3nP.text:
Played roughly 36% of the time is Black's only other option, ...Nxf2.

This really isn't all that great, but you need to know how to punish it.

We'll move our queen to d5.

Similarly to the ...Bxf2+ lines, this move attacks a piece of Black's (the bishop in this case) and allows for a potential cxb7 at the right moment.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2P5/4p3/4n3/2P2N2/PP3bP.text:
Most often, Black takes on f2 with their bishop and checks our king.

Our only legal move is Ke2.

A bongcloud, but up a piece.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bPp3/4n3/2P2N2/PP3.text:
Played 16% of the time is the ultra sharp piece sacrifice with 5...Bc5!

This is where you need to know your stuff. One wrong move from either side can result in total devastation. We will accept Black's offering.

Luckily, Black is the one who is going to have to prove that they have got enough compensation for the piece.

r1bqkb1r/p3nppp/2pp4/1B2N3/4n3/2P5/PP3PP.text:
If Black simply recaptures...

We can capture the c6-pawn with our knight, threatening more discoveries.

r1bqkb1r/pp2nppp/2pp4/1B1PN3/4n3/2P5/PP3.text:
The only reasonable way to proceed is to block the check with ...c6.

We'll continue by taking the c6-pawn.

We are now threatening to win lots of material with cxb7+, so Black has to try to do something about it...

r1bqkb1r/ppp1nppp/3p4/3PN3/4n3/2P5/PP3PP.text:
Shockingly, the most natural way to proceed is a horrible blunder!

6...d6 is played 63% of the time and lands Black into a dead lost position.

It's sort of logical as Black attacks the knight and opens up their bishop. 

But we can punish Black for opening up the diagonal to their king by giving a check with our bishop!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PP.text:
Black responds by developing their other knight to f6 and attacking e4.

This move signifies the Jaenisch Counterattack, which is the most popular response to the Ponziani.

Black's move intends to make use of the fact that we no longer have a convenient way to support e4.

But instead of supporting e4, we'll follow up on our previous move and strike in the center with d4!

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3Pn3/2P2N2/PP3.text:

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/4p3/Q3p3/2P2N2/PP1P.text:
Nearly 47% of games go like this.

White takes on e4. This move is really bad and shows that most people don't know the theory in this line.

We won't recapture on e4. 

We will attack the pinned piece and take on e5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black defends.

And now we go for The Ponziani.

r2qkbnr/pppb1ppp/2n5/4N3/Q3p3/2P5/PP1P1P.text:
5...Bd7 is the most popular: Black unpins and threatens the knight.

However, we can take and then take on e4. 

We will be up a pawn.

r3k1nr/pppqbppp/2n5/8/4Q3/2P5/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
This line is an example of how play could continue.

We push with d4 and gain more space.

We've cleared the center so this is a must.

r3k2r/pppqbppp/2n2n2/8/3PQ3/2P5/PP3PPP/R.text:
Black attacks our queen.

But they do not have nearly enough compensation for the material. 

We are up a central pawn.

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/2n5/8/Q3p3/2P5/PP1P1PPP/.text:
Black recaptures.

And we are up a pawn.

r4rk1/pppqbppp/2n2n2/8/3P4/2P2Q2/PP2BPPP.text:
We can block the e-file and get ready to castle. 

With our pawn advantage there's not much to strategize. 

Play the position and win, using the e-file and the e5-square to get a piece in the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black pushes their e-pawn, too.

We attack the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this last chapter on The Ponziani, we will learn how to play against 3...d5. 

This central pawn challenge is not so popular: only 7% of games, yet it's the most solid way of fighting against The Ponziani.

2kr1bnr/pppq2pp/2n1bp2/3pp3/Q3P3/2PP1N2/.text: Black castles queenside, which falls right into our strategy.

2kr1bnr/pppq2pp/2n1bp2/3pp3/QP2P3/2PP1N2.text:
And one of the benefits of c3 is to play b4, too. 

We will attack the king that is now stuck on the queenside behind all its clumsy pieces.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pp3/4P3/2P2N2/PP1P.text:
3...d5 challenges our e4-pawn.

We will respond with a pin on the c6-knight. 

Here, we also defend e4.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n2p2/3pp3/Q3P3/2P2N2/PP.text:
4...f6, played in around 12% of games, is cutting edge theory.

Black supports the center with the pawn and isn't afraid of weakening their king.

We will play 5.d3 to support e4.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n2p2/4p3/Q3p3/2PP1N2/PP.text:
5...dxe4 is natural. 

Black wants to trade.

We recapture. Our bishop on f1 now has more squares to move to.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black defends.

And now we go for The Ponziani.

r2q1rk1/ppp1n1pp/2nbbp2/4p3/Q2PN3/2P2N2/.text:
Black castles.

We take in the center. 

Our knight is strong on e4, and so 
we don't want to take on d6 right away. 

We can do that later.

r2q1rk1/ppp1n1pp/3bbp2/4n3/Q3N3/2P2N2/PP.text: Black takes on e5 with their knight.

And we castle. 

We also don't mind ...Nxf3+, as we'll just recapture with the bishop. 

This is a stable position in which we'll enjoy some play, thanks to the incoming Rd1.

r2q1rk1/pppb1pp1/3b1n1p/3P2B1/2BPp3/2P5/.text:
If ...h6, we don't take on f6.

We keep the pin and try to get Black to push ...g5.

r2q1rk1/pppb1ppp/3b1n2/3P4/2BPp3/2P5/PP2.text:
Black castles.

We'll play Bg5. Only good things can result from this pin. 

It's pressure that gives Black something to constantly worry about.

r2q1rk1/pppb1ppp/3b1n2/3Pp1B1/2B5/2PP1Q2.text:
We don't mind giving up the bishop here because our control of the key e4-square will increase. 

We want to castle, play Nd2 and potentially even the move a4 if it's useful for queenside space and our bishop's comfort on c4.

r2qk1nr/ppp3pp/2nbbp2/3pp3/Q3P3/2PP1N2/P.text:
This is one of the potential setups that you could see. 

Both bishops out and supporting the central pawns.

Our knight also supports e4. 

We can make use of e4 after all the central pawns are traded.

r2qk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nbbp2/3p4/Q2pP3/2P2N2/P.text:
This trade also leads to another stable position.

We recapture with the knight, centralizing it.

r2qk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nbbp2/3pp3/Q3P3/2PP1N2/.text:
Black develops the other knight to play O-O.

Now breaking in the center is thematic. 

If you see that Black will castle kingside, d4 is a good plan.

r2qk2r/ppp1n1pp/2nbbp2/4p3/Q2Pp3/2P2N2/P.text:
8...dxe4 is possible, but it's not best. 

We will get our knight to e4 quicker.

We take, with an attack on the bishop.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/3Pp3/2B3b1/2P1Q3/PP.text:
When Black defends it, but they also block their queen's attack on d5.

This is still better than giving us the e5-pawn.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/3b1n2/3Pp3/2B3b1/2PPQ3/PP.text:
Once again, 10.d3 is the best way to develop here because our queen is rather restricted on e3. 

We have to defend e4 and make sure we have dominant control over that square.

We want to get a knight to e4, castle and play h3. 

We have a good position.

r2qk2r/pppb1ppp/3b1n2/3P4/2B1p3/2P5/PP1P.text:
Black brings the bishop out.

We can push and gain some space because the e-pawn is pinned.

Black is ahead in development for now, but our space advantage in the center restricts their potential.

r2qk2r/pppb1ppp/3b1n2/3Pp3/2B5/2P2Q2/PP1.text:
With 8...Bd6, Black supports the e5-pawn and prepares castling.

We push 9.d3 to control the e4-square. 

It will also be the funnel through which our pieces are developed.

r2qk2r/pppbn1pp/2nb1p2/3p4/Q2NP3/2P5/PP1.text:
The bishop goes and unpins the knight.

But there isn't a scary discovered attack, so we can just castle.

r2qk2r/pppbn1pp/3b1p2/3p4/3QP3/2P5/PP1NB.text:
But we can simply recapture. 

This is an example of a line Black has to know in order to have a decent position in The Ponziani. 

All of our pieces are ready to handle any trades in the center and attacks.

r2qk2r/pppbn1pp/3b1p2/3p4/Q2nP3/2P5/PP1N.text: Black can take on d4, attacking our queen.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3Pp3/2B3b1/2P2Q2/PP1.text:
Black attacks our queen. 

Luckily, our d5-pawn isn't completely defenseless.

We can move away and attack the e5-pawn.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/5n2/3P4/2B1p3/2P2Q2/PP1.text:
Our queen can be attacked by the pawn.

On e2 we can exert pressure on the e4-pawn.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/5n2/3Pp3/8/2P2Q2/PP1P1P.text:
Black develops their knight to f6 with pressure on d5. 

...Bg4 also becomes possible.

That's why we must defend d5.

r2qkbnr/ppp3pp/2n1bp2/3pp3/Q3P3/2PP1N2/P.text:
The bishop helps support d5 and it clears the way for castling queenside, potentially.

Since our pawn is on d3, we can only develop to e2.

r2qkbnr/pppb1ppp/2n5/3pp3/Q3P3/2P2N2/PP1.text:
4...Bd7 breaks the pin. 

It has been played in around 20% of games.

But we can take on d5 since the discovered attack isn't a problem.

r2qkbnr/pppb1ppp/8/3Pp3/8/2P2n2/PP1P1PPP.text:
The knight takes on f3.

We recapture with the queen.

r2qkbnr/pppb1ppp/8/3Pp3/Q2n4/2P2N2/PP1P1.text:
5...Nd4 is played almost 72% of times. 

It's a discovered attack on the queen but we also have to take care of the c2-square.

The d1-square is the only square for us to defend everything.

r2qkbnr/pppb2pp/2n2p2/4p3/4P3/2P2N2/PPQ2.text:
We of course get out of the way. 

We have an equal position on our hands but we will continue development with Bc4, O-O, Be3 and Nd2.

r2qkbnr/pppb2pp/2n2p2/4p3/Q3P3/2P2N2/PP3.text: This unpins the knight and prepares a discovered attack.

r2qkbnr/pppbnppp/8/3Pp3/8/1QP2N2/PP1P1PP.text:
We can fall back and pressure b7. 

We are up a pawn and have a substantial advantage.

r2qr1k1/pppb1pp1/3b1n1p/3P4/2BPp2B/2P5/P.text: The rook goes to e8 to defend e4 and potentially support the e3-push.

And we castle. 

We want Nd2 and Rae1 because our rook on f1 may become useful if Black chooses to play ...e3 to open up the files.

r3kbnr/pppq2pp/2n1bp2/3pp3/Q3P3/2PP1N2/P.text:
Queen to d7 paves the way for queenside castling.

These positions are generally equal because Black's center is solid.

We castle.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black pushes their e-pawn, too.

We attack the e5-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
For this second study, we will analyze what to play if Black actually knows the best theoretical moves: 4...Bd7 and 4...f6!

We begin with 1.e4.
